title: Use case diagrams
idea: A use case diagram shows who uses a system and which goals they reach with it, so you fix the scope before drawing a single class.
points: A use case is one goal an actor reaches through the system, named verb-first.
Secondary actors are outside systems a use case calls, such as a payment gateway.
«include» is a step that always runs; «extend» adds optional behaviour under a condition.
Each use case has a main flow and alternate flows: your requirements.

steps.caption: Start with actors: roles outside the system that want something. A person can play several roles.
Each actor links to the goal it starts. Name a use case with a verb and an object.
«include» points from the base use case to a step it always performs. Every drop-off pays postage.
Collecting always checks the pickup code. An included step becomes a step inside the method, or a private helper like `pay`.
«extend» points the other way: from the optional behaviour to the base. The fee runs only when a parcel waited too long.
The gateway is a secondary actor: the system calls it. In code it becomes an interface at the boundary.

code.title: The diagram
code.caption: The full diagram as PlantUML text, including the courier's use case. Paste it into a PlantUML renderer to draw it.

walk.text: Actors are roles, not people. The payment gateway is an outside system, so it is an actor too.
The rectangle is the system boundary. Everything inside is in scope; everything outside is not.
Solid lines join an actor to its use cases, including the secondary actor the postage step calls.
`<<include>>` arrows run from the base use case to the step it always needs.
`<<extend>>` runs from the optional extension to the base it can extend.
The courier has its own goal. Each actor's goals hint at a separate client of your API.

code.title: From use cases to code
code.caption: Each use case becomes one method; included steps become private helpers or guard checks; the gateway becomes an interface.

walk.text: The secondary actor is outside the boundary, so the service depends on an interface, not a vendor.
One service exposes the actors' goals. Its methods read like the use case list.
The main flow of "Drop off parcel". The full-lockers check is an alternate flow, written as an exception.
Postage is «include»d: the drop-off cannot finish without calling `pay`.
An unknown code is an expected alternate flow, so it returns `Optional.empty()`.
The «extend» condition is a guarded call: the late fee runs only after the free days.
The run walks the main flow and each alternate flow: full lockers, a bad code, a late pickup.

pitfalls: Drawing internal steps like "save to database" as use cases; keep only goals an actor values.
Reversing «include» and «extend» arrows makes a mandatory step look optional, or the reverse.
Listing only the main flow; alternate flows like a wrong pickup code become your error handling.

quiz.q: A recipient pays an overdue fee only if the parcel waited too long. How do you draw it?
options: «include» from Collect parcel to Pay overdue fee
Make Pay overdue fee a separate actor
«extend» from Pay overdue fee to Collect parcel
A solid line from Recipient to Pay overdue fee only
quiz.why: Conditional, optional behaviour is «extend», drawn from the extension to the base. «include» means the step runs every time, which is wrong for a fee charged only when late.

takeaway: Actors and their goals first; classes come from the use cases.

starters: Where do non-functional requirements like latency go, if not in the diagram?
What is the difference between a use case and a user story?
When does a use case deserve its own service class?
